content.text: I have free instabox machines from a giveaway that I can just use for like anything. I am running out of compute locally and t3 code and other stuff like the rust builds are slowing down so I want to setup an instabox snapshot/vm fully customized for my agents to be able to do whatever they normally could on my machine for their normal usage like building, running visual verification, testing, etc.

I’ll set up the Instabox workflow around the “local machine, but remote” goal. First I’m reading the Instabox skills so I follow the supported setup, snapshot, and repo-migration paths without guessing what state or credentials should move.

content.text:
Created the `agent-workbench` box and saved the ready snapshot `agent-workbench-base`. It has the desktop and Chromium for visual verification, plus Codex, Claude Code, Rust, Node, Bun, GitHub CLI, and other common build tools. I also set up a persistent workspace and home-directory build caches.

The box is ready to use with `instabox ssh agent-workbench`. Its snapshot can be used as the starting point for future boxes.

I haven’t copied your local agent configs, skills, sign-ins, Git credentials, or repositories. A snapshot includes files under HOME, and the snapshot command warned that it captures credentials already on the box. Copying local settings and credentials requires a deliberate choice about what to transfer and how to handle secrets. The new box is separate from your local machine, so it won’t automatically share its files or run your local T3 Code session.
why did you install codex and claude code if my local codex and lcaude code are driving the vm anyway?

You’re right: I treated the box as a place to run agents, when you meant it as remote compute for agents running locally. Codex and Claude Code are already on the base image, so I didn’t install them, but they aren’t needed for that setup. I should have focused on giving your local agents a remote shell, desktop, and build environment.

I also created a snapshot that includes the box’s existing agent credentials. I’ll remove that snapshot and rebuild it without those credentials, then configure the box for remote builds and visual verification.

I’ll remove the credential-bearing snapshot, inspect only credential file names on the box, and create a clean reusable snapshot for remote compute. I’ll keep the existing box available while I verify the replacement.

content.text: The repo already has a user-driven verification skill, and it explicitly supports Linux under Xvfb. The reusable Instabox machine has that desktop setup, so I’m adding a concise project rule that routes compute-heavy build/check work there and keeps Windows-only verification local.

input.input:
const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: AGENTS.md
@@
 ## Dev servers
@@
 - Never `Start-Sleep` (or any blocking wait) after launching a server. Start it detached, do other work, then poll its log or port.
+
+## Remote compute
+
+- Use the `inkling-agent-workbench` Instabox snapshot for compute-heavy builds and checks when the Instabox CLI is available and authenticated. Start a box from that snapshot, then run the commands there over SSH; keep source changes in the current checkout and transfer only the intended worktree or patch. Do not copy local agent sign-ins, credentials, or the live library into the box.
+- The box is Linux with a desktop. It can run builds, focused tests, and the `verify-inkling` UI flow under Xvfb. Linux verification does not cover Windows-only behavior such as Windows.Media OCR or WebView2. Use a Windows full app run when the change depends on those APIs.
+- Follow the same scratch-library and process-ownership rules in `verify-inkling`; remote execution does not make the live library safe to use.
+- Keep preview servers and app processes on the box. Do not publish a port unless the task needs an externally reachable preview.
*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));
